title: Bhumia's promises
hook: tradition says a robber promised Nanak never to lie, harm the poor or betray a host, and the promises changed him

segments.voice: Yesterday, settle here: the unkind village stayed put while the kind one scattered, because goodness spreads. Today, a robber with an open kitchen.

A rich man keeps an open kitchen. Holy men passing through his district eat well at his table and leave praising his generosity. Nobody says aloud where the money comes from: robbery. Bhumia, the sakhis call him, a landholder who raids by night and feeds saints by day. Then Nanak comes through, sits at the table, and doesn't eat. Bhumia wants to know why.
screen: `AN OPEN KITCHEN.` → `PAID FOR BY ROBBERY.` → `NANAK DOESN'T EAT.`

segments.voice: In the sakhi, Nanak tells him plainly: food bought with stolen money isn't something he'll eat. Bhumia says he can't give up robbing; it's who he is. So Nanak, the story goes, asks for something smaller. Three promises. Never tell a lie. Never harm the poor. Never betray anyone whose salt you have eaten, whose food you've shared. Bhumia agrees. Those sound easy. That night he sets out to rob the king's palace, dressed so finely the guards take him for a nobleman. One asks who he is, and he remembers promise one. A thief, he says. The guard laughs and waves him in. Inside, he gathers treasure, and in the dark he tastes something from a dish. Salt. The king's salt. Promise three. He sets the treasure down and leaves with nothing. In the morning the palace finds things moved and nothing taken. The king's men find Bhumia, and asked straight out, he tells the truth. Tellings differ on what the king did next, but they agree the robber was a changed man, and that he found Nanak again and gave up robbery for good. Nanak didn't demand a whole new life at once, only three small promises. They didn't change Bhumia's mind first. They changed what he could do, one night at a time, until there was no room left for the old life.
screen: `STOLEN MONEY, FREE FOOD.` · `THREE PROMISES.` · `A THIEF, HE SAYS. THE KING'S SALT.` · `THE PROMISES LEAVE NO ROOM.` · then, large: `PROMISES CHANGE US.`

segments.voice: Choose one small promise, like Bhumia's: small enough to say yes to tonight, real enough to matter, like I won't lie about this one thing, or I'll keep the confidence a friend gave me. Word it plainly, and say it once, quietly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.
Bhumia's promises. Never lie, never harm the poor, never betray one whose salt you've eaten: the three small promises that, in the sakhi, turned a robber around.

Your line: promises change us. That ends a week of sakhis: the learned man of Benares, Farid's successor, the king of the island, Mardana's last song, the boy who feared the fire, two villages, and Bhumia. Day seven hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs retell the sakhi of Bhumia the robber as a story about honest earning and keeping one's word.

chat.says: How did three small promises change a robber in that sakhi?
options: Keeping them blocked the old life: he told the truth, and after tasting the king's salt, took nothing.
Nanak made him swear off all crime at once, and he obeyed out of fear of punishment.
The king forgave him on the spot, so he no longer needed to steal to feed his guests.
chat.meaning: Never lie, never harm the poor, never betray one whose salt you've eaten: small promises that changed what Bhumia could do.
